title: Why Nightingale Put Fresh Air Into Hospital Design
topic: Why Florence Nightingale instituted the “sanitary pavilion” design for hospitals in London (1854) after observing ventilation effects on soldiers’ recovery

lines: Florence Nightingale walked crowded wards at night, lamp in hand.
Soldiers lay packed together in stale air.
In 1854, the war hospital at Scutari had overcrowding, defective sewers, and poor ventilation.
During her first winter there, 4,077 British soldiers died.
Ten times more soldiers died from illness than from battle wounds.
Nightingale blamed poor nutrition, missing supplies, stale air, and overworked soldiers.
She sent a plea to The Times, begging the government to fix the hospitals.
The new Renkioi Hospital had a death rate less than one tenth of Scutari's.
The Sanitary Commission reached Scutari in March 1855, almost six months after Nightingale arrived.
You see, a packed ward with no fresh air feels like a stuffy room you cannot escape.
Nightingale concluded that poor living conditions killed most soldiers at the hospital.
She collected evidence for the Royal Commission on the Health of the Army.
Her Notes on Nursing turned ventilation lessons into practical advice.
Then she turned to sanitary hospital design, including the pavilion model.
The Sanitary Commission flushed the sewers and improved ventilation.
Death rates fell sharply. Nightingale never claimed credit for the change.
The lamp made her famous. Clean sewers and fresh air cut the deaths.

claims.claim: Nightingale became famous as the Lady with the Lamp, making ward rounds for wounded soldiers at night.

Scutari hospital had overcrowding, defective sewers and lack of ventilation; 4,077 British soldiers died during Nightingale's first winter, and ten times more soldiers died from illness than from battle wounds.
The Sanitary Commission was sent to Scutari in March 1855, almost six months after Nightingale arrived, and it flushed out the sewers and improved ventilation, sharply reducing death rates.
Nightingale never claimed credit for helping to reduce the death rate.
After returning to Britain, Nightingale collected evidence before the Royal Commission on the Health of the Army and then turned to the sanitary design of hospitals.
Renkioi Hospital, built after Nightingale sent her plea to The Times, had a death rate less than one tenth of that of Scutari.
Nightingale's Notes on Nursing turned the Crimean war hospital defects, notably ventilation, into lessons, and the pavilion model of hospital design was central to her hospital reform.
